documents.title: Economic and monetary policy outlook
documents.sourceParagraphs: ["Thank you, Cortney [Cowley], for that kind introduction. I’m delighted to welcome everyone to the Dallas Fed’s Houston branch. It’s great to be here with my colleague Jeff Schmid, president of the Kansas City Fed, and with all of you.","This is the 11th joint energy conference of the Dallas and Kansas City Feds, and it just keeps getting better. In large part, that’s thanks to all of you who join us for this event and share your expertise as speakers and audience members. Thank you for being here. Thank you, also, to everyone at the Dallas and Kansas City banks and on site here in Houston who put in the effort to make this day possible. I’m looking forward to an amazing day of dialogue and learning.","You can’t understand the U.S. economy without understanding energy. Energy is a critical input to practically every industry, from traditional manufacturing to data centers. The cost of energy shows up in everything we buy. The ways we produce and consume energy shape how geopolitics affects America’s future. The Dallas and Kansas City Federal Reserve Districts contribute nearly half of U.S. energy GDP, and our two banks are committed to thoroughly understanding this sector.","At the Dallas Fed, we continue to invest deeply in academic research and industry engagement to inform our thinking. Our publications this year showed how the shale revolution transformed the U.S. response to energy price shocks and examined the ways the data center buildout is moving electricity prices . Through our Energy Advisory Council and other programming, we keep open lines of communication with industry leaders to understand how the energy economy is evolving. That outreach proved vital this year amid fast-moving geopolitical developments with wide-ranging implications for energy markets and the U.S. and world economies. Daron Peschel and Kate Faucher in Houston and Garrett Golding in Dallas lead our energy outreach. I hope you’ll take the opportunity to connect with them today if you aren’t in touch with them already.","Since our last conference one year ago, the price of crude oil has risen close to 50 percent on net. Wholesale diesel prices had doubled at one point, though they have retraced somewhat, and natural gas prices in Europe remain more than twice as high as a year ago. Prices of fertilizer and some other commodities have also soared. One piece of good news for American energy consumers has been the sharp decrease in U.S. natural gas prices. Domestic gas supply surged as the ratio of gas to oil rose in aging shale fields. Although there’s been progress on opening pipelines to bring gas out of the field and to American consumers, export capacity to reach the world market and its higher prices remains limited. Again, though, domestic natural gas prices are one of the few bright spots in the global picture of increasingly expensive energy.","Rising energy prices have contributed to higher inflation. Over the 12 months through September, the most recent data available, the price index for personal consumption expenditures (PCE) rose 3.6 percent.","But recent wartime energy disruptions are far from the only source of price pressures. Inflation has now exceeded the Federal Open Market Committee’s 2 percent target for nearly six years. And looking ahead, inflation appears set to trend meaningfully above that target.","Excess inflation is unacceptable. It hurts families, businesses, taxpayers and the American economy. Congress charged the FOMC with delivering price stability as well as maximum employment. We must fulfill this responsibility. In my remarks today, I’ll describe my outlook for economic activity, employment and inflation, then discuss how I believe monetary policy should adjust to sustainably achieve both of the FOMC’s mandated goals. These are my views and not necessarily those of my FOMC colleagues.","Economic growth is strong. Real gross domestic product (GDP) increased at an annual rate of 3.4 percent in the third quarter. And the Dallas Fed’s Weekly Economic Index is consistent with real GDP continuing to expand at around a 3 percent annual rate. Here in the 11th Federal Reserve District, the Dallas Fed’s Texas Business Outlook Surveys and Energy Survey also indicate ongoing strength.","Two main elements underpin economic growth right now. First, consumer spending is solid, especially among wealthier households that benefited most from the increases in the stock market earlier this year. Recent revisions to data on gross domestic income increased my confidence that households have the resources to sustain consumption at a healthy pace.","Second, business investment is robust. Real business investment in equipment rose 14 percent in the third quarter from a year earlier. Computers, peripherals and communication equipment—the categories used in data centers—make up more than 80 percent of that growth. Investment is broadening, though, as companies build out the artificial intelligence supply chain. In recent months, industrial machinery has accounted for about 5 percentage points of annualized equipment investment growth. That category includes semiconductor manufacturing equipment, gas turbines used to generate power for data centers behind the meter, and electrical transmission and distribution apparatus. Business leaders also tell me manufacturers and defense contractors are ramping up investment. And respondents to the Dallas Fed’s Energy Survey report a pickup in capital expenditures over the past year. Technological innovation and changes in global trade and security alliances appear poised to continue driving strong investment in coming years.","A growing economy creates jobs, and the labor market is balanced and even tightening a bit. Unemployment continues to hover just above 4 percent. That is down slightly from late last year and close to most estimates of the lowest sustainable level. On average, employers are adding more than enough jobs each month to absorb trend growth in the labor force.","Today’s labor market is not especially dynamic. Rapid technological change and geopolitical volatility have increased employers’ uncertainty about their future workforce needs. They don’t want to lose the people they have, but they don’t want to commit to new workers, either. It's a tough market for anyone seeking employment.","As a country, we must ensure the labor market works well for everyone. Monetary policy, however, addresses cyclical mismatches between supply and demand, not structural challenges such as employers’ uncertainties. And the latest data show hints of increased dynamism, including more job openings and more workers quitting their jobs. My assessment is that the economy is achieving maximum employment and, supported by strong aggregate demand, remains on track to continue to do so.","Turning to price stability, the FOMC targets an annual inflation rate of 2 percent as measured by the PCE price index. It’s important to know what it means to target an inflation rate.","In my travels around the region, I’ve learned a lot about the remarkable technologies that make the energy industry so productive. One of those is directional and horizontal drilling. As many of you know far better than I, drillers can land a well bore thousands of feet below the surface and miles from the drilling pad with near-pinpoint accuracy.","This technology especially impresses me as a central banker because inflation targeting doesn’t work like that. Shocks constantly buffet the economy: pandemics, wars, novel technologies, discoveries of new energy resources, changes in consumer and business sentiment, and more. Each shock may cause inflation to rise or fall. No central bank, no matter how diligent, can eliminate all shocks and make inflation exactly 2.0 percent every year. Moreover, the economy does not turn on a dime. When inflation deviates from 2 percent, the Fed can’t immediately bring it back to target, at least not without risking an overshoot in the opposite direction.","But there are two things the Fed can achieve. The FOMC can set monetary policy so inflation is likely to return to target in a timely manner. That is, policymakers can ensure that, looking a couple of years ahead, there are balanced risks of having inflation above or below the target. Second, by delivering on the inflation target and explaining a strategy for doing so, policymakers can give the public confidence that inflation will average 2 percent. When shoppers, workers, business leaders and investors expect inflation to be on target, those expectations establish an anchor that helps keep inflation on target.","As I mentioned at the outset, inflation has now exceeded the Fed’s target for nearly six years. But because monetary policy takes time to affect the economy, what matters for policy decisions today is where inflation is going, not where it’s been.","Unfortunately, inflation is trending meaningfully higher than 2 percent. Identifying the trend in inflation requires looking through temporary factors that cause fluctuations in particular prices. For example, the energy shock from conflict in the Persian Gulf raised inflation this year. That effect will fade as higher energy prices become the new baseline. Indeed, if the fighting ends, falling energy prices could temporarily lower inflation.","At the same time, central bankers must not be too eager to call shocks temporary. Sometimes, a shock kicks off a new trend that will affect inflation for some time. The large language model that underpinned the first public release of ChatGPT in November 2022 has long since been retired. Yet it launched an era of intense innovation and investment whose effects have only grown with time. And while diplomats may settle any one international conflict, the world appears to have entered an era of increasingly frequent tensions. As you in the energy industry know well, these conflicts often disrupt supply chains and drive up prices, on top of the tragic human toll of war.","There is no single best method for determining what’s temporary and what’s a trend in inflation. I combine many methods and indicators to build a more complete picture. Let me give you a tour of what that dashboard shows right now.","One group of methods relies on filtering out noise in the inflation data. Although the FOMC targets the overall inflation rate, headline inflation includes some volatile prices that aren’t good guides to what will happen in the future. Metrics that remove volatile categories or extreme price changes provide better signals of where overall inflation is likely to trend.","For example, core PCE inflation excludes food and energy prices, which have relatively little predictive power for future overall inflation. Core PCE inflation was 3.1 percent over the 12 months through September. The Consumer Price Index for October came out this morning. It was higher than expected. I am concerned that PCE inflation could rise when we receive those data for October in a couple of weeks.","Other measures that filter out volatile or extreme price changes likewise indicate inflation is trending meaningfully above 2 percent target. The New York Fed’s multivariate core trend inflation index registered 2.8 percent in September. The Dallas Fed’s trimmed mean PCE price index has been lower, 2.3 percent on a 12-month basis through September. My staff’s research finds , however, that a change in the mix of price increases and decreases is causing the trimmed mean to drop too many increases right now. This effect likely makes the trimmed mean lower than the true inflation trend.","Another way to assess the inflation trend is to examine which prices are rising. If price increases are concentrated in narrow categories that experienced identifiable shocks, inflation may cool as those shocks pass. By contrast, if price increases are widespread, it is more likely that inflation is elevated at least in part due to an underlying trend.","The data show particularly large price increases over the past year in energy products as well as energy-intensive services, such as air travel. Inflation also remains somewhat elevated in manufactured goods affected by tariffs.","But the pressures are broader than that. Prices for non-housing, non-transportation core services rose 3.2% over the 12 months ended in September. That increase is eight tenths of a percentage point above the pace that has historically been consistent with achieving the FOMC’s inflation target. Non-housing, non-transportation core services include categories like visits to the doctor, childcare, dining out and hotel stays. Prices for these services aren’t particularly sensitive to tariffs, conflict in the Middle East or surging demand for computer chips. While I expect inflation to moderate as price pressures dissipate in energy and manufactured goods, the broader inflationary trend is more likely to persist.","When inflation trends too high while the labor market remains near maximum employment and even tightens, the FOMC is achieving only one of its two goals. Tighter policy will be necessary to appropriately balance the outlook and risks for inflation and employment. And it is important to achieve that balance promptly. The longer above-target inflation persists, the greater the risk that it becomes baked into behavior.","The CEO of a major global manufacturer talked with me recently about his thinking on wage increases for 2027. This CEO grew up working class. He knows what rising gas and grocery bills can do to a family. So, he leans toward raising pay in 2027 to offset the inflation in 2026. Across the economy, nominal wage growth has been subdued the past few years. That kept inflation from being even higher but also meant some workers’ pay fell behind the cost of living. An approach like this CEO described could take some pressure off workers. But if it became widespread, the FOMC would have to slow the economy more to bring inflation back to target. The FOMC should not take that risk.","In my view, accommodative monetary policy is adding to inflationary pressures. Economists have a concept called the neutral interest rate that measures the level where the fed funds rate is neither supporting nor restraining activity. The neutral rate is uncertain. It cannot be directly observed, but it can be estimated with economic models. Across eight published models, estimates of the neutral real interest rate currently range from 1 to 1.85 percent. The fed funds rate is 3.88 percent in nominal terms. To convert that to a real rate, you have to subtract off expected inflation. My staff examined a baker’s dozen surveys measuring inflation expectations over the next year among households, businesses and market participants. The data suggest respondents expect PCE inflation to run around 3.1 percent in the near term, up a percentage point from before the pandemic. That makes the real fed funds rate 78 basis points, or a quarter-percentage-point below the lowest estimate of neutral.","Moreover, broad financial conditions are currently providing a tailwind to the economy. As I said earlier, stocks have risen this year. Credit spreads widened this fall but remain compressed by historical standards. Banks remain eager to lend.","Long-term interest rates have risen significantly so far in 2026, about three-quarters of a percentage point on net in the case of 10-year Treasury notes. But those higher long-term rates do not represent as much of a drag on the economy as you might expect. Rates rose mainly because investors expect stronger nominal growth and higher neutral interest rates. So, the higher market rates are more a message that investors believe monetary policy has work to do than an independent headwind for activity.","There are always risks to the economic outlook. Escalation or de-escalation of the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East could change the path of energy prices, with implications for inflation and demand. Business investment could strengthen or falter as companies learn more about the uses of artificial intelligence and governments consider policies toward this potentially transformative technology. Fiscal policy may change with a new Congress. And forecasts of inflation and employment are just forecasts. They come with uncertainty, and as a policymaker, I’m humble about my ability to predict the future.","But policymakers must make decisions in the face of uncertainty, with the information we have available. I anticipate that without any monetary policy restraint, inflation will continue to trend above target unless unexpected shocks occur. I currently estimate that the fed funds target range is at least 50 basis points—half a percentage point—below the level that would create some modest restriction and begin to bring the inflation trend back to target.","After raising the fed funds target range by 25 basis points in September, the FOMC skipped an increase at our October meeting. Financial markets had been volatile in the weeks before the meeting in response to news on the technology investment outlook and geopolitical developments. In such an environment, adjusting policy more gradually can help households, businesses and market participants adapt to higher rates and reduce the risk that economic activity deteriorates more sharply than necessary. Moreover, as long as market participants understand the FOMC’s policy plans, the precise timing of each rate increase has little effect on the longer-term rates most borrowers pay.","Skipping one meeting does not change the monetary policy destination. Indeed, by making the destination clear, the FOMC can better help the economy adapt and obtain the promised benefits of a skip. It remains clear to me, given the current outlook, that the FOMC needs to implement at least two more 25-basis-point rate increases.","The exact pace of increases could depend on the near-term economic and financial environment. It may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the FOMC has moved so far this fall.","After two more increases are in place, it would make sense in my view to pause and examine economic and financial developments to determine what further action may be appropriate. The goal should be to make policy modestly restrictive so we can sustainably deliver both maximum employment and stable prices. Market- and survey-based measures of long-run inflation expectations are near 2 percent, indicating the public trusts the FOMC to deliver price stability. By communicating and delivering on a strategy for moving to a modestly restrictive stance, the Fed can continue to earn that trust. Of course, I will change my policy views if the economic outlook and risks change.","Thank you for joining us today and for the opportunity to share my views with you. I look forward to our dialogue throughout the day.","Lorie Logan is president and CEO of the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas."]

documents.title: The U.S. Economy and Considerations for Monetary Policy
documents.sourceParagraphs: ["The Federal Reserve, the central bank of the United States, provides the nation with a safe, flexible, and stable monetary and financial system.","Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman","At the C. Peter McColough Series on International Economics Council on Foreign Relations, Washington, D.C.","Vice Chair for Supervision Bowman presented identical remarks at a subsequent event held by Unleash Prosperity Now on the same day.","Good afternoon. It is a pleasure to join you today at the Council on Foreign Relations to discuss my outlook for the U.S. economy.","Economic growth has gained momentum this year, driven by robust investment demand and solid consumer spending, and the labor market now appears to have stabilized. These outcomes suggest that the policy rate cuts toward the end of last year helped to address some labor market weakness. We are experiencing rapid technological change and ongoing geopolitical tensions, while inflation pressures have persisted for longer than I had hoped and have shown recent signs of broadening. Despite these challenges, increased investment in and use of artificial intelligence (AI), or super intelligence, are boosting economic growth and productivity and American families appear to be resilient.","The Federal Reserve's monetary policy goals are to achieve maximum employment and price stability. While the labor market has improved more than I expected this year, our progress on lowering inflation has disappointed. Therefore, bringing inflation down remains a priority. I am also monitoring expectations about AI and energy prices, and how they influence the risks to achieving our mandates. Consistent with my views following our September FOMC meeting, I continue to focus on interpreting the underlying trends in the economy and the evolution of financial conditions.","In my remarks today, I will review our most recent FOMC policy meeting and discuss current economic conditions and my near-term outlook for the economy. I will then turn to recent developments in energy markets and the AI buildout and will conclude with my thoughts on the appropriate path of monetary policy.","Update on the Most Recent FOMC Meeting At last month's FOMC meeting, I joined my colleagues to support holding the federal funds rate target range at 3-3/4 to 4 percent. This approach was consistent with my view that further changes in the policy rate should wait until we had a better understanding of how conditions would evolve and how the recent rate increase would influence the underlying trends in the economy. Maintaining the policy stance at the October meeting allowed us to assess the incoming data. While I continue to expect that several of the factors currently boosting inflation will abate next year, currently inflation has proven to be more persistent than I had anticipated. It is also important to gain greater clarity on the effect of recent market volatility on financial conditions.","Economic and Financial Conditions U.S. economic growth has stepped up this year. After rising a solid 2.4 percent during the first half of the year, real gross domestic product (GDP) likely increased at an even stronger pace of more than 3 percent in the third quarter, well above last year's 2 percent pace. Economic growth has been supported by robust increases in AI-related capital expenditures and solid consumer spending. However, some interest-rate-sensitive sectors like residential investment have declined, and the recent rise in mortgage rates appears to be dragging home construction and sales down further. Consumer spending has strengthened this year, despite softness in real incomes and declining sentiment, which are partly due to higher energy prices.","Labor Market Conditions Labor market conditions look to have improved since last year. Over the course of this year, the unemployment rate has edged down to 4.1 percent in October, remaining close to my estimate of its natural rate. Job gains have been above last year's anemic pace, averaging about 80,000 per month through October, and have broadened across industries beyond health care and social assistance.","The labor market continues to show low dynamism, with low-hiring and low-firing conditions as we sometimes see in a late-cycle expansion. The job-finding rate has been low, especially for new labor force entrants, and the share of long-term unemployed workers has moved up significantly. Workers' perceptions of job availability in the Conference Board survey have remained soft in recent months. On their own, these data would be consistent with a higher unemployment rate than currently reported. However, layoffs have moved down this year, offsetting the softness in hiring. In plain terms, workers are both less likely to find a new job and less likely to be laid off, a somewhat unusual pattern.","Although stable, the labor market does not appear to be tight, as wage growth has slowed to a modest pace. On a 12-month basis, the wages and salaries component of the employment cost index increased 3.1 percent in September, the same pace as the change in average hourly earnings for October. Both measures have slowed noticeably from a year ago. An increasing number of workers have taken on a supplemental part-time job to make ends meet, as the share of multiple job holders has increased back to levels seen in early 2025. Given strong productivity gains in recent years, wage growth at this pace is in line with or even below the pace we would expect if inflation was running at 2 percent.","Inflation Progress on lowering inflation has stalled over the past two years or so. Today's consumer price index suggests that 12-month core PCE inflation likely moved up further to 3.3 percent in October, as upward pressures from higher energy prices and AI-related demand continue to flow through to core goods and services prices.","Lack of progress on lowering inflation largely reflects a confluence of shocks unrelated to conditions in the labor market. Tariffs, energy, and AI-related price pressures each accounted for roughly one-fourth of above-target core PCE inflation over the 12 months ending in September. The remaining one-fourth likely reflects persistent effects from the inflationary shocks in recent years. Price pressures had been concentrated in a few categories, but the latest data suggest that these pressures may be broadening.","It is important to ensure that those inflationary pressures do not intensify, further broaden, or become embedded in consumer and business expectations. But today's consumer price index data suggest that inflation pressures may persist for longer. Tariff effects should further wane going forward. Energy-related price pressures should unwind when the Middle East conflict resolves. And inflation pressures related to the AI buildout seem to persist despite some early signs of slowing. I mostly view these pressures as reflecting relative price shocks in specific sectors of the economy. For example, the AI buildout has quickly shifted investment demand toward specific types of high-tech capital, putting upward pressure on prices due to relatively inelastic supply in the near term. As these shocks wane or unwind and with no inflationary pressures emerging in the labor market, my forecast is for core PCE inflation to move closer to 2 percent next year.","Financial Conditions Financial conditions have tightened a bit recently because of lower equity prices, higher private interest rates, and a stronger dollar. That tightening comes against a backdrop of increased market volatility. Corporate bond and mortgage rate spreads have widened, and equity valuations in the tech sector have dropped, as investors appear to be reassessing expected returns and the risks associated with increased external financing for AI investment projects.","Economic Outlook and Risks Looking ahead, my expectation is that policies designed to boost the economic potential of the U.S. economy would continue to support productivity, growth, and business confidence. These policies include pragmatic regulations, lower taxes, and more supportive policies toward businesses. I expect the labor market to remain stable and inflation to slow, as special factors currently holding inflation elevated gradually wane or unwind next year. Over time, I also expect increased AI adoption to raise productivity and put some downward pressure on inflation as lower production costs are passed through to consumer prices.","On risks to the outlook, with the labor market improving since last year, I am more attentive to the inflation side of our mandate. Sustained supply-chain pressures from the AI buildout or greater pass-through of higher energy costs could cause inflation pressures to persist. I can also envision a scenario in which the effects of the Middle East conflict and the tech investment boom wane or unwind quickly. In this scenario, I would also expect a timelier return of core PCE inflation toward our target.","I also see a number of risks to the outlook for economic activity, many originating in financial markets. These risks include a large correction in equity valuations, if returns on AI investment fall short of expectations, and a sharp increase in private longer-term interest rates. Lower equity prices could undermine the resilience in consumer spending. And higher interest rates could further strain interest-rate-sensitive sectors of the economy, like housing and small business investment. I will continue to closely monitor developments in credit and equity markets to assess risks to economic growth and financial stability.","Important Issues for Monetary Policy I see conditions in energy markets and the AI buildout as two important issues for the economy in the months ahead. Developments in these two areas could have material effects on both sides of our mandate and could influence my views on the path for monetary policy.","Energy Markets The Middle East conflict has disrupted energy markets, impairing the flow of oil and other commodities passing through the Strait of Hormuz, which accounted for about 20 percent of global oil supply before the conflict—roughly equivalent to total U.S. oil consumption. As tensions rose, Brent oil prices moved up to and above $110 per barrel in the second half of October before dropping sharply last week on optimism that an agreement between the U.S. and Iran could be reached following the midterm elections. Although crude oil flows in the Persian Gulf have recovered to near pre-conflict levels in recent weeks, freight rates and insurance premiums have surged because of more complex logistics and ongoing geopolitical risk, raising the cost of delivered oil to many markets around the world.","Prices for gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel also moved up to near or even above their highs in the spring. These higher prices reflected both higher crude oil prices and wider refining margins, as refineries in both the Persian Gulf and Russia have been damaged as a result of ongoing military conflicts in both regions. Prices for refined products have retraced some of the earlier gains more recently as crude oil prices have receded and margins have shown signs of normalizing.","While the outcomes of these conflicts remain uncertain, my approach is to look through temporary energy-driven inflation, when possible, and to remain alert to signs that it is spreading into broader prices or expectations. If geopolitical tensions persist, energy prices may stay elevated in the near term, increasing risks that core inflation may also stay elevated because of increased pass-through to consumer prices of higher production and transportation costs.","Although the U.S. economy is now a net exporter of oil products and less energy intensive, we could still see an impact on economic activity from higher energy prices. The recent deterioration in consumer sentiment measures suggests households may be internalizing a more persistent reduction in their purchasing power. I would be especially concerned about effects on both sides of our mandate if there were further significant disruptions to energy markets. An escalation of geopolitical tensions could have more meaningful effects on real activity because of higher uncertainty and the larger impact of energy prices on lower- and middle-income consumers.","Even with a quick resolution to the Middle East conflict, it may take some time for energy prices to normalize. Futures markets expect oil prices to decline only gradually, as global oil consumption is projected to exceed supply at least through the end of this year. As inventories have been drawn down, the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) has reached a bit less than 50 days of crude oil imports, the lowest level since the early 1980s, reflecting both this year's and the larger 2022 SPR releases. A number of new Gulf pipelines to bypass the Strait of Hormuz are under construction or expansion, with the United Arab Emirates' West–East expansion coming online in early 2027 and most others in 2028 and beyond. Domestic oil production could also continue to rise, which would put downward pressure on fuel costs.","AI Buildout In remarks earlier this year, I discussed the responsible use of AI in the financial system. Today I will describe how this technology is shaping the broader economy. Given the transformative promise of this technology, investment in data centers has boomed and has been a major influence on the U.S. economy. With plans for new data centers continuing to surge, I expect the AI shock to play out over some time. However, as these investments are increasingly being financed with external funds, including off-balance-sheet liabilities, I am also focused on potential risks to the economy and financial stability if revenues from AI customers disappoint.","We may still be in the early days when investment rises rapidly while workers and firms determine the best use cases before we see more meaningful effects on productivity. The boom in data center investment is undeniable, with growth in real business fixed investment strengthening further this year to a pace like the 1990s tech boom. High-tech equipment, software, and data center construction have accounted for the large majority of growth in business investment since 2025, with gains broadening to other categories this year.","AI adoption has grown significantly, especially among larger firms, with about 25 percent of businesses and roughly 10 percent of workers reporting using AI every day in their work. However, use varies greatly across industries and occupations, with stronger adoption in information and other business services sectors. I think there is a risk that some workers will be displaced as firms adopt this technology, even as others see their productivity—and wages—rise. Monetary policy cannot address that transition directly, but it should support a dynamic labor market that facilitates the necessary retraining and mobility of workers across jobs.","AI revenues have been rising quickly but are not yet sufficient to pay for the expense of maintaining existing and developing new AI models and data centers. As capital spending has surged, hyperscalers and other companies have increasingly been sourcing funds from credit and equity markets. And as investors see an increased risk in these investments, the cost of financing has been rising notably.","In addition to financing costs, the AI buildout is also putting upward pressure on a number of price categories. Prices of memory chips, semiconductors, computers, and other electronic products have increased sharply this year—in a few categories by double digits—as demand from data centers has outpaced supply. I expect production capacity to catch up to demand gradually over time.","AI-related debt has been rising rapidly, with notable gains in corporate bonds, private credit, and project finance, and is on track to exceed $800 billion this year. Other obligations, in the form of long-term lease and contract commitments and residual value guarantees, have also surged and their potential payments are estimated at more than three times the amount of debt. Given their strong credit ratings, hyperscalers and large tech firms have assumed off-balance-sheet liabilities to allow smaller and riskier companies to use them as collateral in asset-based financing for data center construction and the purchase of accelerated computing equipment. These connections among AI firms have also been accompanied by hyperscalers and chip designers making equity investments in smaller companies that purchase their products, creating the appearance of circular financing.","The largest U.S. bank holding companies have some exposure to AI-related financing, which is scrutinized during annual supervisory stress tests. Life insurance companies, pension funds, private credit, and mutual funds also have exposure. Most of these entities are well capitalized and have stable funding. But the complex nature of the financing structures makes it difficult to properly assess counterparty risk.","Risks seem to be concentrated in only a few large firms that provide AI services, including AI labs and the hyperscalers. If AI-related revenues fall short of sharply rising costs, especially as public sentiment and local opposition could lead to increased regulation and delays, we could see a sharp correction in equity prices for AI firms, higher financing costs, and reduced access to credit. This shock would likely slow the AI buildout and soften both economic activity and inflation.","We may have already seen some reassessment of expected returns play out in recent weeks as equity valuations dropped, corporate bond spreads widened, and credit default swaps increased for some companies involved in the AI buildout. I will be looking at how momentum in adoption of and investment in this technology evolves and for possible effects on both inflation and employment.","The Path Forward for Monetary Policy As we think about the path ahead, it is important to remember that over the past two years the U.S. economy has experienced successive inflationary shocks that have not been driven by labor market conditions. Monetary policy cannot offset the direct effects of tariffs and energy costs on inflation, but it plays a central role in containing the second-round effects. Monetary policy also has limited influence on AI-related price pressures. However, in certain segments of AI-intensive sectors, particularly among newer and medium-sized firms, higher interest rates appear to be holding back investment and purchasing decisions.","As I noted earlier, financial conditions have tightened. Against this backdrop, the benefit of additional policy tightening has to be carefully weighed against its costs for interest-rate-sensitive sectors. The October Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey on Bank Lending Practices (SLOOS) suggests that the concentration of demand weakness in real estate loan categories reflects existing headwinds in those sectors.","Time will help us learn more about the durability of momentum in AI-related demand and the evolution of geopolitical risks, both of which could be critical in the months ahead for setting our policy stance. Greater clarity on AI-related financing conditions and the sustainability of AI investments should increase my confidence in future policy decisions. Geopolitical conditions affect commodity markets and the degree of economic uncertainty perceived by households and businesses.","Before our next meeting in December, we will receive the PCE inflation report for October and the employment report for November. Today, I am seeing signs that inflation pressures are persisting, while labor market conditions appear to be firming. This indicates that there is still work to do to bring inflation closer to 2 percent. Given the recent market volatility, I will also continue to closely monitor how developments in financial conditions influence the economic outlook.","In the meantime, I will continue to meet with a broad range of contacts to inform my assessment of economic conditions and the appropriate stance of policy. It is important to remember that monetary policy is not on a preset course. At each FOMC meeting, my colleagues and I will evaluate incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the implications for the risks to our dual-mandate goals of maximum employment and price stability.","Thank you again for the invitation to join you this afternoon. I look forward to our discussion.","1. documents.sourceParagraphs: ["The Federal Reserve, the central bank of the United States, provides the nation with a safe, flexible, and stable monetary and financial system.","At the Bank of England Watchers Conference King’s Business School and Money, Macro and Finance Society, London, United Kingdom","Thank you, Paul, and welcome to Bank of England watchers, who I suspect are watching the Federal Reserve as well.","My subject today is the outlook for the U.S. economy and the implications for monetary policy. I think there is little disagreement about the basics of that outlook. The U.S. economy is growing strongly, with a labor market that has brought employment close to its long-term rate. But inflation remains too high, so I will explain why I believe further tightening of monetary policy will be needed, sooner rather than later, to return inflation to a path that will reach 2 percent in the medium term.","The outline of my speech is to first explain why I voted to hold the policy rate steady at the most recent meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). Then I will talk about the general state of the U.S. economy. After that, I will ask some open-ended questions about the dynamism of the U.S. labor market that are important to consider over the longer run. I'll follow that by a discussion of recent inflation data and then describe my views about the future path of monetary policy.","At our most recent meeting, I supported the FOMC majority in holding monetary policy at its current setting. As I said in a speech a couple weeks before then, my rationale was that the Committee's communication about the likely tightening of policy had already led financial markets to price in some tightening. When this communication is clear and credible, what really matters is that those hikes are eventually carried out—it is not necessary, for example, to raise rates at consecutive meetings.","If, however, the hikes are not carried out, markets will reduce expectations of rate hikes and rates will immediately fall, which would loosen monetary policy in an undesirable way. So, while the precise timing of the hikes doesn't matter, ensuring that the promised hikes are implemented in a reasonable period of time does.","Let me turn to the economy. Economic output continues to grow at a healthy pace. The initial estimate was that real gross domestic product (GDP) rose 3.4 percent in the third quarter, supported by strong consumer spending and robust investment. Consumption growth was helped by a booming stock market, and investment by businesses continued to surge, especially in high-tech equipment associated with the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout. I expect GDP growth is backing off a bit in the current quarter, as consumer spending slows to levels that I think are more consistent with household income and wealth, but output will continue to grow at a solid pace.","The labor market has also been solid. The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1 percent in October, the same rate it was over the summer. Job creation, which has been fluctuating widely month to month for some time, saw October gains of 165,000 jobs and 85,000 jobs added to estimates of the previous two months. To look through the volatility, the 6-month and 12-month average payroll gains have been closer to 80,000 jobs a month. This level is a bit above most estimates of the breakeven level needed to keep the unemployment rate steady but entirely consistent with my view that the supply and demand for labor are in rough balance.","While the labor market has been stable, for over a year now it has been what is best characterized as \"low hire, low fire.\" One can understand this characterization by looking at job separation and hiring rates today and comparing them with what they were before the pandemic (see figures 1 and 2 ). You will see that the rate of separations, the sum of layoffs and quits, has been persistently low the past few years compared with a decade ago. The hiring rate is also low. This is unusual because, in a strong labor market, the hiring rate is usually high. Hiring tends to be low when the labor market is weak, which is when the firing rate is often elevated. What is unusual today, and may be unprecedented, is the extent to which both firing and hiring are now so low.","These data have led me to consider a question that has longer-term implications for the economy and monetary policy: Does a stable labor market necessarily mean it's a healthy labor market? To illustrate the difference, if your mom was in the hospital and the doctor told you her condition was stable, you would be relieved but you wouldn't say she is healthy. I am concerned that the low hire, low fire equilibrium in the labor market means it has lost some of its dynamism, which is important for productivity growth and real wages. If the labor market is in fact showing less dynamism, is it an issue for monetary policy? While I don't have answers to these questions, I do think the questions are worth asking.","This discussion starts with distinguishing between net employment growth and gross flows in and out of employment. Behind the monthly job creation numbers that get most of the world's attention is the enormous churn in the labor market. For example, the 60,000 jobs created in September was a net change in the level of employment, but it is dwarfed by the more than 5 million people who left their jobs that month and the more than 5 million who were hired. Despite the low separation and hiring rates, the level of separations and hiring is huge. When I was a professor, I would use the following analogy for my students. If you stand by a river, you can measure the water level. If you return the next day and measure again, you will likely find that the water level is unchanged—it is stable. But in fact, a massive amount of water has flowed downstream since the day before. The same goes for the labor market—there is a lot of churning even if the level of employment is stable.","The question is, does churn in the labor market matter? If so, is labor market churn bad or good? One could argue that this churn is inefficient. Why are people and firms wasting time swapping workers across jobs? If workers simply stayed at their firms, and firms never let them go, employment would be stable and resources would be saved from putting workers into new jobs. But would it mean the labor market is healthy?","The answer is that the churn in hiring and firing is actually good for the economy. This churn reflects a dynamic market that allows labor resources to be allocated to more productive uses. If a worker and firm are not in a good, productive match, then it is more efficient and better for the economy for the worker and firm to separate and look for new partners. When more productive matches are formed, productivity, real wages, and profits will be higher. In this situation, employment may not be stable, but it is healthier.","I believe this churn is what leads to the exceptional performance of the U.S. economy. The relative ease of starting businesses in the United States, compared with many other advanced economies, is a big advantage. The relative ease of firing employees, compared with many European Union economies, is surely not welcome by the workers affected, but cumulatively it was a factor that drove the stronger recovery in the United States from the pandemic recession. This flexibility in hiring and firing promotes a better match between skills of the worker and those demanded by businesses, making the most productive use of their abilities. As a result, this churn boosts the capacity of the economy and allows incomes to grow without inflationary pressure.","So, given this discussion, how do we interpret the current low hire, low fire economy? Does it indicate that the U.S. labor market has become less dynamic and less healthy, which has implications for the economic outlook and for monetary policy? I will first consider the possible causes of this lower dynamism and then the possible implications.","One explanation for the lower dynamism is that some of the decline in both hiring and firing may reflect, in part, a continuation of longer-run trends that were in place even before the pandemic. First, it is well known that the workforce is aging for a number of reasons: People are living longer and are healthier and more active at older ages; many members of the large post–World War II baby boom are in their 60s and 70s; and birth rates have declined, which increases the relative age of the workforce. This aging affects the dynamism of the labor market because older workers switch jobs less frequently, since many have managed over time to find better job matches and because older workers are less likely to relocate for work. The second trend is that the level of education of the workforce is increasing over time. More educated workers experience less job churn in general and, during downturns, face lower rates of job separations. Since 2010, the share of adults 25 and older with at least a bachelor's degree has increased from 28 percent to 37 percent.","If these were the only reasons for the decline in labor market dynamism, then it would be at a level consistent with these trend factors, suggesting an appropriate degree of dynamism with no implications for monetary policy. But the data suggest that, even after accounting for these factors, labor market dynamism still seems somewhat low. There are several possible reasons.","One is that hiring and job-switching may have been restrained by the confluence of factors that have raised economic uncertainty since early 2025: the advent of AI, tariffs, changes in immigration policy and enforcement, and a general level of uncertainty about the economic outlook that has made business planning particularly challenging. One piece of evidence was a special question posed in the Federal Reserve's November 2025 Beige Book survey of economic conditions: Employers reported in November 2025 that hiring was unusually restrained because of uncertainty. I don't think uncertainty has diminished much since then. And another piece of evidence is in the most recent Beige Book, showing that several Fed Districts reported firms had delayed hiring or anticipate less job creation after investing in AI.","Another reason for low dynamism is that low firing may be a consequence of the huge surge in job-switching from 2020 to 2023 related to the pandemic. Workers in new jobs are less inclined to change jobs again, and that may be limiting job-switching. If this is a large factor, it may be temporary—workers are in their jobs for a median of three years before switching again, and we are nearing that threshold for the last of the pandemic job switchers. But it's possible they could be staying longer now if the job-switching triggered by the pandemic had been unusually effective at improving the matches between workers and jobs—many relocated or chased dreams and new careers and may not be as willing to switch again.","As you can tell, it is hard to pin down and properly weigh the possible causes of lower labor market dynamism and then judge how long that phenomenon might continue. This makes it hard to know the implications for the economic outlook and monetary policy.","But we can talk more constructively, I think, about the possible effects of the current low hire, low fire environment. While low layoffs imply that fewer workers experience unemployment, a low hiring rate means that those who do become unemployed may experience longer unemployment spells. And, in fact, the percentage of unemployed people who have been looking for work for more than six months has climbed steadily since 2022 and is now quite elevated for a period of economic expansion. Another logical consequence of lower dynamism in the labor market would be that new entrants, typically young and with less experience, are having a harder time finding jobs. I think anyone paying attention to the U.S. economy has been hearing about the challenges young workers are facing. Indeed, the share of new labor force entrants in unemployment has been rising and has reached close to the highest levels of the past twenty years.","Both these developments may reflect a labor market that is not as healthy as the headline unemployment rate indicates, with implications for the longer-term path of monetary policy. If hires and separations are low because worker matches have improved, then this may be a boost to productivity and can be largely ignored in assessing the state of the labor market. But I worry that today's labor market dynamism may be low due to impediments to mobility that are affecting long-term and youth unemployment, and this may lead to a less-efficient distribution of workers across jobs, hindering productivity growth. This possibility is important to monitor because productivity growth is a crucial factor in judging how fast the economy can grow without undesirable inflationary pressure. As I said earlier, I don't have the answers to the questions I have posed, but I believe the questions are worth asking and addressing with more research.","Let me put aside this discussion about the health of the labor market for now. What is important in the near term is that I see the labor market as stable and employment at a level close to the FOMC's maximum-employment goal.","By contrast, inflation is well above 2 percent and the focus of my attention. For reasons I explained at the start of this speech, I was willing to wait to tighten monetary policy at the FOMC's October meeting. Inconveniently for today's event, we will get consumer price index (CPI) inflation for October in a few hours. While I am hoping for an improvement over September, even if this occurs, I would still support a 25 basis point increase in the FOMC's policy rate at our December meeting. However, if inflation comes in substantially higher than I expect, more robust action by the FOMC may be called for.","Let's just say it. September's inflation data were bad. There was no silver lining. Inflation based on personal consumption expenditures (PCE), the measure targeted by the FOMC, rose at a monthly rate of 0.5 percent in September and 3.7 percent over the previous 12 months. Core PCE inflation, excluding food and energy prices, rose 0.3 percent in September and 3.1 percent from that time last year. Both these measures are too high, and I am particularly concerned about the breadth of price increases. Earlier this year, excessive inflation was driven by nonmarket prices that are estimated rather than observed by the government, and ones that I tend to discount as hard to measure and as an unreliable guide to the overall trend for core inflation. But now, two components with greater relevance to future inflation are elevated—core goods prices and those for core market-based services excluding housing. More than 70 percent of the components of core PCE service prices saw 12-month increases above 3 percent in September.","Later today, I will be looking to see whether this breadth of elevated inflation continues, including whether high-tech goods prices related to the AI buildout continue to rise at the very high rate of recent months. I also want to know if the run-up in energy prices of the past several months is being passed through to goods and services directly or indirectly, because of higher input costs. While I am pleased to see energy prices down from their high rates over the past week or so, they are still quite elevated relative to the start of the year, and the ultimate effect on inflation will depend on what levels are sustained.","Federal Reserve staff have been thinking hard about the effects on inflation of the AI buildout and elevated energy prices, and their findings do not encourage me to think that these factors will be fading anytime soon.","In one exercise, researchers tried to capture imminent price pressures with a textual analysis of the well-known surveys of purchasing managers conducted by the Institute for Supply Management (ISM). ISM surveys ask purchasing managers to list specific commodities, materials, and services whose prices rose or fell that month. Staff used these responses to construct monthly price pressure indexes that correspond with actual categories of the producer price index (PPI). They found these indexes provide information about future changes in producer prices and, as a result, should have some signal about future PCE inflation. For example, the index for high-tech products rose in December 2025 and jumped further in January 2026, ahead of an escalation in those goods prices that eventually showed up in the February PPI and inflation data. The most recent ISM data, for October, point to the possibility of more price increases ahead.","Some other Fed research indicates to me that energy price pressures may pass through to goods and services in a more sustained way than in the past. The researchers find a potential shift in the inflation process after the pandemic that suggests core inflation may be more responsive to energy shocks. Central bankers have tended to look through energy price shocks and expect that their effects on inflation will soon fade, but this new work cautions against taking too much comfort in this view. Their analysis suggests that, especially if oil prices were to remain elevated, these pressures could be larger than previously though and persist well into 2027.","And there are reasons to also expect elevated energy prices to persist. First, even as there is increased tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, that traffic is moving at great expense. The insurance now needed for ships making this passing, and the ship-to-ship transfer of oil necessary to guard against Iranian attacks, are reportedly boosting oil prices by $20 to $30 a barrel. A second problem is that diesel oil production is affected by limited refining capacity and other constraints. As a consequence, elevated prices for diesel in the United States are not expected to moderate as readily as crude oil prices would in a more peaceful Middle East.","To recap my economic outlook, economic activity is strong, the labor market is stable, but inflation is too high, well above the FOMC's 2 percent goal. This means that even if, as I expect, the monthly rate of inflation improves in October, I am leaning toward supporting an increase in our policy rate of 25 basis points at the FOMC's December meeting.","That's my plan if things proceed as I expect. But if the October CPI inflation data out later today are similar to the past two monthly readings—with core CPI inflation around 0.3 percent or even higher—then a stronger policy move may be needed. In that case, I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting. Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take.","1. documents.title: Economic Outlook
documents.sourceParagraphs: ["Philadelphia Fed President and CEO Anna Paulson shared her economic outlook at the 81st Annual Field Meeting Capstone.","Good evening, everyone, and thank you, Joe. It's a pleasure to be with all of you for the 81st Field Meeting Capstone.","Tomorrow is Veterans Day, so I'd like to take a moment to thank the veterans with us tonight, and everyone who has served.","I also want to thank everyone who has shared insights about economic conditions with us over the past year. Your stories illuminate what the data can't show.","Through roundtables, surveys, and conversations with our team, you've helped all of us better understand what's happening in the economy and what it means for communities, households, businesses, and financial institutions.","And there's been a lot to understand. Before I share my thoughts on the economy and monetary policy, I want to emphasize that, as always, these are my views. They don't necessarily reflect those of other members of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) or the Federal Reserve.","The data, and what I hear from all of you, tell me the U.S. economy is strong, and stronger than many had anticipated.","Back in December of last year, the median FOMC participant expected GDP to grow 2.3 percent this year. So far, growth has averaged 2.7 percent.","In December, the median participant expected the unemployment rate to end the year at 4.4 percent. The economy has overperformed here, too. The unemployment rate was 4.1 percent in October, and hiring has been broad-based.","What about inflation? At the end of last year, the median participant expected inflation to ease this year to 2.4 percent. As you all know, that hasn't happened. Instead, inflation has gotten worse. PCE inflation, the Fed's preferred measure, was 3.6 percent over the 12 months ending in September.","This year has brought strong growth and healthy hiring. It has also brought elevated inflation. I'll talk about each of these in turn. Then, I'll turn to monetary policy, where getting inflation back to 2 percent remains my priority.","Let's start with growth. Artificial intelligence (AI) gets a lot of the headlines, and AI-related investment is certainly important. But the economy's strength is broader than AI. In our October survey of manufacturers here in the Third District, every business, 100 percent, planned to increase or maintain capital spending next year. That is very rare. In fact, it has only happened in 20 months going all the way back to 1968. And 10 of those months have come in the last year.","The U.S. consumer is also playing an important role in this year's strong growth. Real consumption growth has averaged 2.8 percent so far this year. That's despite average real income growth of just 1.3 percent. A combination of borrowing, drawing down savings, and spending out of investment gains likely explains the gap between consumption growth and income growth.","Turning to the labor market, the data show we have been close to what I consider to be maximum employment for several years. And the labor market has strengthened in 2026.","Last year, job gains averaged just 10,000 per month and were heavily concentrated in healthcare and social assistance. This year, average monthly job gains have been 86,000, and job creation has been much broader. We've also seen healthy hiring in transportation and warehousing, construction, and professional and business services.","Wage growth has been about 3 percent. But with inflation even higher, many workers feel as though they are falling behind.","That brings me to prices. Inflation has been above the FOMC's target of 2 percent for five and a half years. Since dropping to 2.3 percent in April 2025, headline PCE inflation has climbed. It has been above 3 percent since March of this year, and the most recent reading, for September, was 3.6 percent.","Today’s Consumer Price Index (CPI) release for October suggests inflation pressures are still very much with us. Total inflation, the headline number, affects everything from how far a paycheck stretches to what a business can buy with its investment dollars. And the FOMC's mandate to deliver stable prices is about headline inflation.","But to understand where inflation is going, which is what matters for monetary policy, we need to look at what's driving it. Three main factors have been keeping inflation elevated: tariffs, energy prices, and the AI buildout.","Tariffs caused goods prices to rise significantly. But recent New York Fed research suggests the inflationary effects of tariffs peaked in February of this year and are beginning to fade. That doesn't mean prices are falling. It just means tariffs are no longer pushing prices up.","Since the start of the war in the Middle East, the average price of a gallon of gas has increased by about 35 percent. Diesel is up more than 60 percent. The knock-on effects of higher energy prices are showing up in services like airline tickets and in inputs like fertilizer.","The AI boom is also adding to inflation. Demand for chips, power generation equipment, and other components tied to the buildout has surged. That demand has pushed up prices for a wide range of goods, from consumer electronics like laptops to raw materials like copper.","So, tariffs, energy, and AI have all been pushing prices up. Tariffs look like they're fading. Energy supply and AI demand pressures are harder to call. What matters for monetary policy is where inflation ends up once the effects of these shocks run their course.","That's why I'm focused on measures of underlying inflation. They show where inflation stands once we set aside shocks that are expected to fade. Ideally, they reflect fundamentals, like the pace of growth and the economy's capacity to produce. They give us a better read on the balance between supply and demand.","There are many ways to gauge underlying inflation, and they all point to the same conclusion. It has been stuck between 2.5 and 3 percent. Some measures are a touch lower than a year ago, and others are a touch higher. But the bottom line is clear. Underlying inflation is above target, and it hasn't come down. That tells me that elevated inflation isn't just about factors that will go away on their own.","At the same time, there are some bright spots. Wage growth is not adding to price pressures. And financial markets expect inflation to return to 2 percent.","But the risks are still high. We've had five and a half years of above-target inflation. And that experience can seep into how businesses set prices and how workers and employers negotiate wages.","We've heard some isolated reports of firms considering larger wage increases to address the cost of living. There's nothing in the data to suggest this is widespread. But it's a development I'll be watching, since it could complicate the path back to 2 percent if it spreads.","So, what does all this mean for monetary policy?","I continue to believe monetary policy needs to be somewhat restrictive to bring inflation back to 2 percent. I supported the decision to raise rates in September, and I supported the decision to hold rates in October. Let me be clear: Skipping a meeting is a matter of pace, not direction. There is likely more work to do.","But I prefer to tighten gradually when conditions allow. Let me explain why, first as a general principle and then as it applies today.","In general, I see two main reasons to move gradually.","First, it gives households, businesses, and the financial sector time to adjust. Families have to work higher rates into their budgets. Businesses have to rethink their borrowing and investment plans. And financial institutions, especially community banks, need time to manage the effects of higher rates on funding costs, loan pricing, and their customers' ability to repay. Gradual steps make these adjustments easier.","Second, moving gradually lets me learn as we go. I can keep gathering data and hearing from businesses about how the economy is adapting before deciding on the next step.","In addition, conditions can change. In the past week or so, we've seen big swings in the stock market and in oil prices. Some of the strength in consumer spending is tied to the stock market, and that may prove less durable than we expect. If it does, the labor market could feel it. Moving gradually lets me adjust as these forces evolve.","But we don't always have the luxury of moving gradually. I would want to act more quickly if inflation expectations drift up, if wage pressures build, or if underlying inflation moves higher. Right now, that's not what I’m seeing. Long-term expectations are well anchored, and wage pressures have been limited.","A gradual approach also works best when the direction of policy is well understood. If markets expect more tightening, moving gradually doesn't leave us behind where we need to be. That's one of the things I’m tracking.","For now, further gradual tightening seems appropriate. But the exact path will depend on how conditions evolve, and I'll be watching the data closely. I'll also keep listening to all of you because, as I said at the start, your stories illuminate what the data can't show.","What won't change is my commitment to the Federal Reserve's dual mandate. Price stability and maximum employment are the conditions families, businesses, and communities need to plan, to invest, and to get ahead. Delivering them is the Federal Reserve's job, and I'm committed to getting it done.","Thank you all so much for coming tonight.","Joe Budash, senior director of engagement and operations, financial institutions relations, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, https://www.philadelphiafed.org/our-people/joe-budash .","Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise, and David E. Weinstein. “How Fast Do Tariffs Pass Through Into Consumer Prices?” Liberty Street Economics (Federal Reserve Bank of New York), October 6, 2026, https://libertystreeteconomics.newyorkfed.org/2026/10/how-fast-do-tariffs-pass-through-into-consumer-prices/ ."]

documents.sourceParagraphs: ["Thank you, Professor [Fred] Smith, for that kind introduction. I’m delighted to be back at Davidson. This institution gave me a firm foundation for my career as an economic policymaker, and I hope it does the same for many of you.","Earlier this week, I participated in the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting in Washington. Before we turn to our conversation on careers and leadership, I’d like to give you a brief update on the economic and monetary policy outlook. These are my views and not necessarily those of my FOMC colleagues.","Congress gave the FOMC a dual mandate. We set monetary policy to achieve both maximum employment and stable prices. Importantly, policy takes time to influence the economy. We therefore set policy based on where the economy is headed, not just where it is today. The Fed’s main monetary policy tool in normal circumstances is the target range for the federal funds rate. So, at our meetings, the FOMC assesses where employment and inflation are headed and debates whether and how to adjust the fed funds target range to best accomplish our mandated goals. I’ll walk you through how I approached that assessment at this week’s meeting, where I voted to maintain the current target range of 3.75 to 4 percent.","Economic growth is strong. Consumer spending is solid, especially among wealthier households that have benefited most from the soaring stock market. And business investment is robust. While data centers get the headlines, manufacturers, defense contractors and energy companies are also ramping up investment.","A growing economy creates jobs, and the labor market is balanced and perhaps tightening a bit. Unemployment continues to hover just above 4 percent. That is down slightly from late last year and close to most estimates of the lowest sustainable level. On average, employers are adding at least enough jobs each month to absorb trend growth in the labor force.","Although the labor market is balanced, it is not dynamic. Rapid technological change and geopolitical volatility have increased employers’ uncertainty about their future workforce needs. They don’t want to lose the people they have, but they don’t want to commit to new workers, either. Companies are slow to hire and slow to fire. This job market hurts new graduates just starting their careers and anyone who needs to find a job. As a country, we must ensure the labor market works well for everyone. Monetary policy, however, addresses cyclical mismatches between supply and demand. Monetary policy can’t fix structural problems such as employers’ uncertainties. My assessment is that the economy is achieving maximum employment and, supported by strong aggregate demand, remains on track to continue to do so.","Turning to price stability, the FOMC aims for an annual inflation rate of 2 percent as measured by the price index for personal consumption expenditures, or PCE. We have missed that goal for nearly six years. While inflation has come down from the post-pandemic peak, it is not yet headed all the way back to our target.","This is unacceptable. Higher prices drain the wallets of parents buying groceries to feed their kids and young people paying rent on their first apartments. Unpredictable increases in input costs make it more difficult for companies to plan investments and create jobs. And inflation burdens taxpayers who finance public services, schools and the national defense. We must restore price stability.","The FOMC targets the overall inflation rate, but headline inflation includes some volatile prices that aren’t good guides to what will happen in the future. Measures that drop these volatile prices or extreme price changes provide better signals of where overall inflation is likely to trend. For example, core PCE inflation excludes food and energy prices, which have relatively little predictive power for future overall inflation. Core PCE inflation was 3.1 percent over the 12 months through September, and higher for the most recent month. (Although these data were released the day after the FOMC meeting, accurate predictions based on other data series were available at the time of the meeting.) The data show broad price pressures across many goods and services, not just those affected by temporary factors such as tariffs and the energy shock. Other measures similarly indicate inflation is trending meaningfully higher than the FOMC’s 2 percent target.","When inflation trends too high while the labor market remains balanced, the FOMC is achieving only one of its two goals. How should monetary policy adjust to fix that?","Very few institutions, and no human beings that I know of, borrow or lend money at the fed funds rate. Car loans, mortgages and business debt all typically use long-term interest rates. The fed funds target range influences the economy by influencing these long-term interest rates and other broad financial conditions.","Financial conditions are currently providing a tailwind to the economy. Stocks, as I said, have risen notably this year. Credit spreads widened in recent weeks but remain compressed by historical standards. Banks remain eager to lend.","Long-term interest rates have risen significantly so far in 2026, nearly a full percentage point in the case of 10-year Treasury notes. But those higher long-term rates do not represent as much of a drag on the economy as you might expect. Rates rose mainly because investors expect stronger nominal growth and higher neutral interest rates. So, the higher market rates are more a message that investors believe monetary policy has work to do than an independent headwind for activity.","There are always risks to the economic outlook. Escalation or de-escalation of the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East could change the path of energy prices, with implications for inflation and demand. Business investment could strengthen or falter as companies learn more about the uses of artificial intelligence and governments consider policies toward this potentially transformative technology. And forecasts of inflation and employment are always just forecasts; they come with uncertainty, and as a policymaker, I’m humble about my ability to predict the future.","But policymakers must make decisions in the face of uncertainty, with the information we have available. I anticipate that without any monetary policy restraint, inflation will continue to trend above target unless unexpected shocks occur. I currently estimate that the fed funds target range is at least 50 basis points—half a percentage point—below the level that would create some modest restriction and begin to bring the inflation trend back to target.","After raising the fed funds target range by 25 basis points in September, the FOMC skipped an increase at our meeting this week. Financial markets have been volatile in response to news on the technology investment outlook and geopolitical developments. In such an environment, adjusting policy more gradually can help households, businesses and market participants adapt to higher rates and reduce the risk that economic activity deteriorates more sharply than necessary. Moreover, as long as market participants understand the FOMC’s policy plans, the precise timing of each rate increase has little effect on the longer-term rates most borrowers pay.","And skipping a meeting does not change the monetary policy destination. Indeed, by making the destination clear, the FOMC can better help the economy adapt and obtain the promised benefits of a skip. It remains clear to me, given the current outlook, that the FOMC needs to implement at least two more 25-basis-point rate increases. After that, it would make sense in my view to pause and examine economic and financial developments to determine what further action may be appropriate. The end goal should be to make policy modestly restrictive so we can sustainably deliver both maximum employment and stable prices. Of course, I will change my policy views if the economic outlook and risks change.","I am grateful to Sam Schulhofer-Wohl for assistance in preparing these remarks.","Lorie Logan is president and CEO of the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas."]
